John Lambert
jŏn lăm´bẽrt
n. (John Lambert, d. 1538, English priest burned at Smithfield after disputing on the Lord's Supper before Henry VIII in person, whose last word was “None but Christ”)
English Lambert, from Germanic Landberht, land-bright; his family name was Nicholson.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

John Lambert was a Cambridge man, chaplain to the English merchants at Antwerp, and twice examined for heresy before the case that killed him. In November 1538 he was brought to Westminster to dispute the bodily presence of Christ in the sacrament, and Henry VIII himself presided, seated in white silk, with Cranmer and Gardiner among the examiners; the king pressed him personally and ten bishops argued against him in succession through the afternoon. Asked at the end whether he would live or die, he committed his soul to God and his body to the king's clemency, and was burned four days later. The accounts say he lifted his hands out of the fire crying “None but Christ, none but Christ.” The doctrine he died for is Heb 10:12, that this man “after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God,” and 1Co 11:24, “this do in remembrance of me.” Joh 6:63 is the verse the Reformers pressed against a carnal eating: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing.”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines transubstantiation as the change of the bread and wine in the eucharist into the body and blood of Christ; a conversion maintained by the Romish church.

expand to see more

TRANSUBSTANTIA'TION, n. The change of the bread and wine in the eucharist into the body and blood of Christ; a conversion which the Romish church maintains to be effected by the consecration.

EU'CHARIST, n. The sacrament of the Lord's supper; the solemn act of ceremony of commemorating the death of Christ.

COMMEM'ORATE, v.t. To call to remembrance by a solemn act.

Key Scripture

Heb 10:12 — "But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;"

1Co 11:24 — "And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me."

Joh 6:63 — "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life."

Mat 26:26 — "And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body."

Modern Corruption

A king sat in judgment on the Lord's Supper and a priest was burned for the answer, which is what happens when a sacrament is made a test of loyalty.

expand to see more

Transubstantiation is the error Lambert died denying, and the Reformed objection is not squeamishness about mystery but Heb 10:12 and Heb 10:14: Christ offered one sacrifice, for ever, and sat down. A rite that re-presents that offering daily contradicts the finished work, and a doctrine that locates Christ's body bodily on ten thousand altars contradicts the ascension. 1Co 11:26 fixes the sense of the ordinance: “as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” — a showing forth until a coming, which presumes He is not bodily here.

Two further errors must be refused in the same breath, and the Reformed position is not a middle muddle but a definite doctrine. Rome's transubstantiation and the Lutheran sacramental union both place Christ's body in or under the elements; bare memorialism empties the sacrament of Christ altogether. Scripture gives a real spiritual presence received by faith, so that the believer truly feeds on Christ while the bread remains bread. Joh 6:63 is the hinge, and the Supper is a means of grace precisely because the Spirit quickens and the flesh profiteth nothing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anamnesis (G364), a remembrance; soma (G4983), body; zoopoieo (G2227), to quicken.

expand to see more

Greek anamnesis (G364) — a remembrance, a calling to mind; 1 Corinthians 11:24.

Greek soma (G4983) — a body; 1 Corinthians 11:24, Matthew 26:26.

Greek zoopoieo (G2227) — to make alive, to quicken; John 6:63.

Greek ephapax (G2178) — once for all; Hebrews 10:10 and the sense of 10:12.

Greek eulogeo (G2127) — to bless; Matthew 26:26.

Usage

"“after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12) — the finished work."

"“this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24) — the ordinance's own account of itself."

"“It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63) — against a carnal eating."
